kernel: Write me an interactive story. Surprise me.

shape.note: through_lines is how many distinct story lines (each with its own ending) the shape preference suggests; the review decides whether each next one is worth building.

protagonist.who: You are the new night assistant in a municipal archive’s reading room, hired to shelve a returned book before the building closes.
protagonist.wants: to understand what the book is and get the room back to an ordinary library before the building’s nightly close finishes it.
protagonist.can_do: read, examine, move shelves, talk to the night archivist and the night custodian, open the book’s pages, and use the room’s levers and passages.
protagonist.cannot_do: open the central book without the night key, move the central reading chair, or make the night archivist accept what the page says without showing her a fact she can check against the room itself.

arena.description: A circular reading room in the basement of a municipal archive: long shelves, a central reading table, a bookcase that is a door, a wall crack at the corner, and a book that should not be on the shelf.

pressure.description: The building is closing for the night: the lamps dim in stages, the shelves lock, and the book’s final page is left open for the night.
pressure.clock_or_stock: none tracked; the night is told through lamp-out stages and rearrangements, because 3-0c names no failure

opposition.who_or_what: the building’s mechanism, administered by the night custodian
opposition.wants: to close the book and file the current reader so the room can rest
opposition.means: it moves shelves, locks doors, dims lamps, repeats the phrase, and can make the companion correct the same false fact

events.what: You open the returned book and find a page describing the reading room exactly, including your position at the center table; when you look up, the page has added a line about what you just did.

The lights fail for a minute; when they return, the shelves have shifted, the central table has moved to the corner, and the night archivist points at a crack in the wall and jokes that it spells READ, while the letters actually spell READER.
The last lamp goes out for good; when it comes back, the central chair is occupied by a page that has your name on it, and the book is open to the blank page.

hidden_truth.truth: The reading room is a machine that files people as pages. The recurring phrase 'the reader is in the center of the room' is not a description but a job title: whoever stands at the center when the book closes becomes the next page. The night archivist is not wrong because careless; she is a copy of the previous reader, and the copy keeps correcting the same fact because the original is already filed.
hidden_truth.who_knows: the mechanism, and the night custodian, who has been closing the book each night to keep the copies from noticing
hidden_truth.what_it_changes: the choice is no longer about shelving a book but about choosing who stands at the center: you, the archivist, or the custodian, and whether the book is opened or closed

mediation.question: Do you let the room finish its work, or do you stop it before it files you?

to_reach_pole_a.what_you_must_do: get the book to the central chair, have the companion correct the false fact, use the crack word to open the bookcase door, and stand at the center when the last lamp dims
to_reach_pole_a.cost: the room files whoever is at the center; the companion’s copy is lost, the custodian’s night shift ends, and you become a page

to_reach_pole_b.pole: stop the room before it files you
to_reach_pole_b.what_you_must_do: return the page to the book, move the central chair out of the center, and convince the companion to read the crack word backwards so the mechanism closes without a reader
to_reach_pole_b.cost: the room forgets what it was for; the book is shelved, the archivist stops correcting the same fact, and the building’s nightly close becomes ordinary

levers: the crack in the wall that spells READER

complications.description: The night key is not on the key ring; it is the small brass plate in the returned book's cover, and the book will not open to the final page unless it is used.
The night archivist's correction is not a mistake: she says the same false fact because the fact is true in the room she was filed in.
The night custodian has been closing the book each night to keep the copies from noticing, and he will not say which copy is next.

cast_seeds.wants: to correct the false fact in the record and restore the room's order
cast_seeds.holds: the knowledge of the room's previous state and the ability to identify discrepancies in the text
cast_seeds.edge: is a copy of the previous reader and does not know she is a copy, believing her corrections are her own expertise

framework.name: Kishotenketsu
framework.shape: a situation is introduced and deepened without conflict, an unexpected element recasts it, and the two are reconciled

modifier.name: Episodic middle
modifier.effect: Each middle beat is a self-contained instance of the story's recurring decision with its own small ending; what carries across them is what the protagonist is becoming.

framework.reading: The story begins in a quiet, ordinary library and deepens as the room's strange logic reveals itself, moving from curiosity to a tense, surreal realization that the reader is being filed. It should land on a quiet, ambiguous reconciliation where the room's nature is accepted or resolved, rather than a dramatic confrontation or victory.
framework.why: The brief specifies no failure presence (3-0c.failure_presence) and a sustained trajectory (3b.primary_trajectory), which aligns with Kishotenketsu's lack of central conflict and its reliance on deepening situation. The 'Reconciliation' beat matches the required 'quiet, ambiguous resolution' (3c.moral_valence), whereas three_act and save_the_cat require climaxes or mirrored finales that contradict the brief's low-stakes, measured tone.

beats.name: Introduction (ki)
beats.job: the people and the place at rest: what an ordinary day here is

beats.name: Development (sho)
beats.job: the same situation, deepened: more of what was introduced, with no new conflict required

beats.name: Turn (ten)
beats.job: an unexpected element or viewpoint that recasts what came before

beats.name: Reconciliation (ketsu)
beats.job: the turn and the earlier material are brought together into a new whole

T1.title: The Reader in the Center
T1.motivation: You start out wanting to shelve the returned book and hand the reading room back to an ordinary nightly close, and by the end you want the people in the room to stay people, even if that means the room stops being what it was.
T1.strategy: You use the room's own record against itself: you check the page against the shelves, the crack, the lamp, and the chair, and you make Brisa Penhallow correct the fact she has been repeating because the record is all she has.
T1.turning_point: When Brisa Penhallow's repeated correction turns out to be the record of a reader who has already been filed, you stop trying to make the room ordinary and start deciding who, if anyone, it will file.

ending.title: An Ordinary Close
ending.summary: The book is shelved, the central chair is out of the center, and the building closes as a plain municipal archive. It costs the room its purpose and the page that might have been you.
ending.changed: the reading room is no longer a filing machine; the book is shelved and the nightly close is ordinary

T2.title: The Archivist’s Page
T2.motivation: You start out wanting to shelve the returned book and finish the night, but once the page adds your name you come to want the room to keep working long enough to prove that its record can be corrected; by the end you want Brisa Penhallow to be the reader the room files, because her corrected certainty is the only thing that can stop the page from adding you.
T2.strategy: Let Brisa Penhallow check the page’s added line against the shelves, the central table, and the crack, let her correct the page’s false line, and keep the corrected page at the center table so the room treats her as the reader it is filing while you hold the lamp and keep the key from Cadhla Marrack.
T2.turning_point: The corrected page at the central table. Once Brisa Penhallow has checked the page against the room, the room no longer treats you as the only reader; it begins to pull her copy toward the center.
T2.differs_from: T1 stops the room before it files anyone and leaves both companions standing in an ordinary archive; this line lets the room finish its work by filing Brisa Penhallow, leaves Cadhla Marrack standing with his shift saved, and leaves the archive still working as a room that adds lines.

ending.title: The Archivist’s Page
ending.summary: The room finishes by filing Brisa Penhallow instead of you: her page takes the central chair, her fact stops being corrected, and the building closes as a working archive that still adds lines. Cadhla Marrack saves his shift and leaves with the key, and the room’s purpose remains intact.
ending.changed: the central chair remains in the center occupied by Brisa Penhallow’s page; the room keeps adding lines instead of becoming an ordinary archive

divergence.trigger: you show Brisa the page’s added line and let her check it against the room
divergence.instead_of: you held the page against the room and matched each line to the shelves, the central table, and the corner crack yourself
divergence.shift: The page has added your name under the line for the reader, and Brisa Penhallow checks the added line against the room and corrects the false part of it. Her correction makes the page stop adding you for a moment, so you come to want the room to keep working under her correction rather than stopping it before it files you.

T2.why: The seed holds as given: N02’s unused way 2 gives Brisa Penhallow the page before the room recasts the situation, and her corrected certainty becomes the line’s own engine. The seed’s ending world also holds, because turn 3’s way 2 and turn 4’s way 2 pay for Cadhla Marrack’s standing by filing Brisa Penhallow instead of you.

T3.title: The Locked Chair
T3.motivation: You start out wanting to shelve the returned book and finish the night, but once the shelves are locked and the crack has spelled READER, you come to want the key without giving the room your page, because the page is the only thing that can still name you as the reader; by the end you want the room stopped before it files you, even if stopping it means no one can open it again.
T3.strategy: Move the central chair out of the center before Cadhla Marrack can file the page, take the key from the locked chair, and make Brisa Penhallow read the crack backwards while the shelves close around you.
T3.turning_point: The chair’s lock. When you move the chair out of the center, the room does not treat it as furniture but as the key’s housing: the chair stays locked in the corner, the shelves close, and the night key comes free only with the room’s mechanism half-stopped.
T3.differs_from: T1 keeps both Brisa Penhallow and Cadhla Marrack and makes the building ordinary; this line keeps only Brisa, loses Cadhla, and leaves the room sealed and frozen rather than plain. T2 lets the room finish by filing Brisa and keeps Cadhla’s working archive; this line stops the room before it files anyone and freezes the room itself, with Cadhla gone and the chair locked.

ending.title: The Locked Chair
ending.summary: The room stops before it files you, but the chair stays locked in the corner and the shelves close around the building; Brisa Penhallow reads the crack backwards and the mechanism freezes with your page still in the book. Cadhla Marrack leaves with the key, and the room becomes a sealed room that no one can open again.
ending.changed: the central chair remains locked in the corner and the shelves are closed for good, so the room is stopped but not ordinary

divergence.trigger: you move the central chair out of the center before Cadhla Marrack files the page
divergence.instead_of: you give Cadhla Marrack the page with your name
divergence.opportunity: The central chair’s lock is shown to hold the night key’s brass plate, so moving the chair releases the key and locks the chair in place.
divergence.shift: The page with your name is still in the book, and the room has not yet filed it; when you move the chair, the shelves lock and the chair stays fixed in the corner, so the key is no longer a way to let the room finish but a way to stop it before it names you.

T3.why: The seed works as given: N04’s unused third way gives the line its own price—moving the chair before the page is filed—and that price carries into the ending, where the room is stopped rather than made ordinary. The ending world differs from both existing lines: T1 keeps both companions and leaves a plain archive, while T2 lets the room finish by filing Brisa; this line keeps Brisa, loses Cadhla, and leaves the room sealed around a locked chair.

promises.reading: The Kernel asks for surprise, which is a demand for the unexpected to feel inevitable. The audience wants to be dropped into a specific, vivid world where the rules are strange but consistent, and to discover that their own competence is the key to a puzzle they did not know they were solving. They want the thrill of recognition: the moment the weird becomes personal.
promises.player_fantasy: To be the one person in a strange room who notices the detail everyone else misses, and to realize that the strange thing is not a monster but a mechanism, and that you are the only one who can operate it.

promises.what: a room that is not what it appears to be: a library that is actually a stomach, a train car that is actually a coffin, a house that is actually a clock
promises.why: the core surprise of the genre; the setting itself is the riddle

promises.what: a recurring object or phrase that seems meaningless at first but becomes the key to the entire situation by the end
promises.why: the texture of discovery; the player feels smart for connecting dots they didn't know existed

promises.what: a companion who is competent but wrong in a specific, consistent way, forcing the player to correct them
promises.why: connection to others is the thematic axis; the companion is the mirror that shows the player their own assumptions

promises.what: a moment of physical danger that is solved by knowledge, not strength
promises.why: the player's competence is the weapon; the stakes are high but the solution is intellectual

promises.what: a quiet, ambiguous resolution where the truth is revealed but the cost is left unstated
promises.why: the moral valence demands quiet ambiguity; the surprise is in what is left unsaid

set_pieces.scene: the player opening a book and finding a page that describes the exact room they are in, including the player's own position
the companion pointing out a crack in the wall and laughing it off, while the player realizes the crack is spelling a word
the lights going out and the room rearranging itself in the dark, so that when they come back on, the player is in a different part of the space

promises.tone_engine: Measured: the prose is calm and precise, which makes the strange elements feel more unsettling. Surprise is produced by withholding information until the player has formed a false certainty, then revealing the true shape of the situation in a single, quiet sentence.
obligatory_cast: a companion who is confident and wrong, providing the contrast that highlights the player's insight
a presence that is not a person but a system, manifesting as changes in the environment rather than a character

plan.assessment: T1 answers pole_b: you stop the room before it files you, keep both the night archivist and the night custodian, and leave the building as an ordinary municipal archive with the room’s purpose destroyed. Missing are a pole_a world where the room finishes its work by filing someone, and a pole_b world where the cost is Brisa rather than the room itself. The story can part early at N02, when Brisa checks the page against the room and the record stops being only yours.
